paper_title: InfoVis: Unified Slide Image Generation and Editing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generating and editing presentation slides requires models to combine accurate text rendering, instruction following, visual grounding, aesthetic design, and precise editing within one canvas. Existing work covers only subsets of these capabilities and lacks large-scale slide-native supervision and diagnostic evaluation. We formulate four slide-centric tasks and build a scalable data engine with over 13M continual-pretraining records and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records. We also introduce VisSlideBench, a benchmark of 1,527 manually screened instances that covers all four tasks with task-specific, multidimensional evaluation. Its automatic rankings agree with blinded, dimension-wise human rankings. Using these resources, we train InfoVis, a unified 9B slide generation and editing model. On VisSlideBench, InfoVis leads every evaluated open-source model on all eleven metrics and scores 7.94 overall against 7.99 for Nano-Banana-2. Starting from FLUX.2-klein-base-9B, slide-specific post-training adds 1.6 points overall, with the largest generation gains in content faithfulness; the remaining gap to proprietary models is smallest in content faithfulness and largest in aesthetic quality. Built on InfoVis, our document-to-slide workflow achieves the second-highest Aesthetics score on the external SlidesGen-Bench. We will release the model, code, data, and benchmark.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Image generation has rapidly expanded beyond natural-image synthesis toward structured, text-rich visual content, including posters, advertisements, infographics, and presentation slides (Wang et al., 2025c; Peng et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025). Slides are particularly demanding because capabilities often developed separately must work together reliably within single canvas. Models must render text accurately, arrange heterogeneous elements into coherent layouts, incorporate supplied visual assets faithfully, and apply local or global edits while preserving unrelated content. Recent open-source image generators have made substantial progress (Black Forest Labs, 2025; Z-Image Team, 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2025), yet they still combine these capabilities unreliably. Accurate, polished, and controllable slide generation and editing therefore remain difficult. major obstacle is the lack of slide-native supervision and diagnostic evaluation. General-purpose image generators are trained on broad visual distributions, with limited supervision for the content layoutdesign relationships characteristic of presentation slides. Meanwhile, existing benchmarks primarily target programmatic or deck-level presentation generation, or include slides only as subset of broader visual-content tasks (Ge et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). These settings do not systematically isolate the capabilities required for single-slide image generation and editing. Equal contribution. Core contributor. Corresponding author.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 1: Overview of our slide tasks, InfoVis, and VisSlideBench. InfoVis is trained through three stages on four generation and editing tasks, and VisSlideBench evaluates each task along taskspecific dimensions. Bar values are the dimension means of Tables 1215. In this work, we cast slide creation as unified conditional visual synthesis problem and study four tasks under shared text-and-image interface: text-to-slide generation, template-conditioned generation, multi-image grounded generation, and instruction-based slide editing (Section 3.1). The tasks share requirements for accurate content rendering and coherent visual composition, while visual inputs serve as style references, content assets, or source slides to edit, which motivates supporting all four within unified model. Figure 1 summarizes our data, model, and benchmark. This shared view directly shapes our data design. We build scalable slide-native data engine that combines real presentations with synthetic supervision and covers the conditioning requirements of all four tasks. Its instructions range from concise user requests to detailed descriptions and structured style_json specifications, so that one model serves both human-facing and machine-generated design conditions. Editing pairs come from deterministic PPTX transformations with instructions derived from the executed changes, complemented by model-generated targets for open-ended visual transformations. The resulting resource contains over 13M continual-pretraining records and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records. To systematically diagnose slide generation and editing capabilities, we introduce VisSlideBench, benchmark of 1,527 manually screened instances dedicated to single-slide image generation and editing across all four tasks. VisSlideBench measures complementary dimensions of slide quality. It evaluates generation in terms of Content Faithfulness, Instruction Following, and Aesthetic Quality, and editing in terms of Semantic Consistency and Presentation Quality. The generation track spans the same three prompt settings as the training data. The automatic evaluators dimension-wise rankings agree with blinded human judgments. Using these resources, we train InfoVis, unified 9B slide generation and editing model based on FLUX.2-klein-base-9B (Black Forest Labs, 2026). On VisSlideBench, InfoVis reaches an overall score of 7.94, leading every evaluated open-source model on all eleven metrics, against 7.99 for Nano-Banana-2 (Google, 2026). Our analysis yields three findings: the gains come from slidespecific supervision rather than scale, as InfoVis is trained from FLUX.2-klein-base-9B and outperforms the 32B FLUX.2-dev; unification costs little relative to our own task specialists, unlike existing unified open-source models, which trail specialists by wide margin; and the remaining

Our main contributions are: We formulate four slide generation and editing tasks and build slide-native data engine with over 13M continual-pretraining and 1.9M supervised fine-tuning records. We introduce VisSlideBench, benchmark for single-slide image generation and editing that covers all four tasks with task-specific, multidimensional evaluation. We develop InfoVis, unified 9B model that leads every evaluated open-source model on all eleven VisSlideBench metrics, scores 7.94 overall against 7.99 for Nano-Banana-2, and is the best open-source model on BizGenEval Slides. sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Structured Rich-Text and Design Image Generation Visual text generation methods improve text fidelity through specialized glyph, position, layout, and text-attribute representations (Ma et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; 2024; Tuo et al., 2024b;a; Shuai et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2026). Building on these advances, recent datasets and models extend text-aware generation to dense and paragraphlevel scenarios (Wang et al., 2025b;a). Beyond rendering text accurately, another line of work studies the generation of complete design images, including posters, product advertisements, infographics, and slides (Wang et al., 2025c; Peng et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2026). Related work also studies factual consistency during structured visual generation and editing (Zhuo et al., 2026), emphasizing that visual quality must be coupled with faithful content realization. General-purpose generators (Black Forest Labs, 2025; Z-Image Team, 2025; Wu et al., 2025) and unified generationediting models (Deng et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026) handle diverse inputs but lack slide-native supervision, while the methods above typically optimize isolated visual artifacts and do not jointly address slide-specific template conditioning, multi-image grounding, and instruction-based editing. InfoVis unifies these capabilities in slide-centric generator with shared content, layout, and design supervision. Benchmarks for Slide Generation Existing benchmarks evaluate slide generation from complementary perspectives. SlidesBench (Ge et al., 2025) focuses on programmatic single-slide generation, while EvoPresent (Liu et al., 2025) evaluates end-to-end paper-to-presentation systems. PPTBench (Huang et al., 2025) covers PowerPoint understanding, modification, and generation, whereas BizGenEval (Li et al., 2026) treats slides as one category of broader commercial visual content. More recent benchmarks, including PresentBench (Chen et al., 2026), SlidesGen-Bench (Yang et al., 2026), and DECKBench (Jang et al., 2026), introduce fine-grained evaluation protocols for slide generation: SlidesGen-Bench separates content, aesthetic, and editability criteria for reproducibility, and DECKBench further extends evaluation to multi-turn slide editing. These benchmarks nevertheless remain centered on complete presentations and agentic workflows, and provide limited diagnosis of individual slide capabilities. VisSlideBench instead targets single-slide image generation and editing, evaluating text fidelity, template consistency, visual grounding, and edit preservation with task-specific protocols and metrics.

sections.title: 3 TASK FORMULATION AND SLIDE DATA ENGINE
sections.content: Our slide data engine recovers slide content and visual elements from presentation pages and converts them into task-specific conditions while keeping the complete slide as the target; editing data instead comes from controlled changes to editable slides. The four tasks thus share content, layout, and design supervision. Appendix gives statistics and implementation details. Figure 2 summarizes the construction.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 2: Slide data engine. (A) Continual pretraining: real decks are filtered, parsed into text and localized visual assets, and annotated with short requests, detailed descriptions, and style_json; the same target slide yields text-to-slide, template-conditioned, and multi-image records, and executed PPTX edits yield sourceinstructiontarget triplets. (B) Supervised fine-tuning: NanoBanana-2 synthesizes targets from LLM concepts, SlideShare content, and paper-derived slide specifications; multi-image records reuse assets extracted from synthesized targets; editing records combine selected CPT triplets with model-generated theme switching and image replacement.

sections.title: 3.1 TASK FORMULATION
sections.content: We formulate slide creation as conditional visual synthesis = Gθ(x, I) over textual condition and optional input images I. In text-to-slide generation, = ; in template-conditioned generation, is reference slide that specifies the visual style; in multi-image grounded generation, holds one or more visual assets that must be preserved in the composition; in slide editing, is the source slide and the requested change, with unrelated content kept stable. Generation instructions take three forms: short caption, detailed description of content and visual design, and structured style_json of the page composition; editing uses natural-language instruction. The same interfaces serve data construction and evaluation, so the training tasks align with VisSlideBench.

sections.title: 3.2 CONTINUAL PRETRAINING DATA
sections.content: Real-slide sources and parsing. We collect real presentations from two complementary sources: author-released conference talks with dense text, equations, and scientific figures, and broader collection spanning 39 topical categories with more diverse templates and styles. We use Qwen3.527B (Qwen Team, 2026a) to remove low-quality and non-slide content, then parse the retained pages with PaddleOCR-VL (Cui et al., 2025) into text in reading order and localized visual elements, which form the shared content representation for the generation tasks. Generation task construction. From each parsed slide, we construct three generation views that share the original rendered slide as the target while using different conditioning inputs. An open

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: VLM generates short request, detailed description, and structured style_json specification from the slide, its OCR transcription, and extracted visual elements. Text-to-slide records use the textual condition alone; the instruction therefore describes the whole slide, visual assets included. Template-conditioned records pair the target with an adjacent slide from the same deck as the reference; we retain pairs with consistent backgrounds, colors, typography, and decorative styles. Multi-image grounded records reuse one to four localized visual elements as conditioning inputs and describe how they should be incorporated into the slide. Executable editing pairs. For editing CPT, we construct sourceinstructiontarget triplets through executable changes to PPTX files drawn from real editable presentations and synthetic PPTX files built from OCR text and presentation backgrounds. Seven operations cover text modification, block addition and removal, background updates, and changes to color, font, and typography; each is executed in the PPTX file and rendered, and an LLM describes the realized change from the source image, target image, and executed action. We remove source slides with layout or rendering defects and pairs with failed edits or inconsistent instructions. Across the four task branches, continual pretraining contains over 13M records.

sections.title: 3.3 SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING DATA
sections.content: Generation SFT. Generation SFT content comes from three sources: LLM-generated concepts across diverse domains, structured content from real SlideShare decks, and research papers converted into slide-level specifications. Nano-Banana-2 renders the content into target slides under diverse visual styles; for template-conditioned generation, we first obtain reference slide from curated template library or by asking Nano-Banana-2 to create one, then generate the target from the reference and new content. For multi-image grounded generation, we extract charts, tables, and other visual regions from the synthesized targets as conditioning inputs. Qwen3.5-27B annotates the records with short requests, detailed descriptions, and structured style_json specifications, or with instructions describing how the assets should be incorporated, and we filter invalid inputs and inconsistent instructions. Editing SFT. For the seven executable operations, we select high-quality triplets from the editing CPT pool by semantic consistency and presentation quality, and add theme switching and image replacement examples generated by Nano-Banana-2 from filtered real slides, recaptioned so that each instruction describes the realized change. Across the four task branches, the SFT resource contains about 1.9M records (Appendix A.4).

sections.title: 4.1 BENCHMARK TASK SUITE
sections.content: VisSlideBench (Figure 5 in Appendix B) evaluates the generation and editing of individual slide images across the four tasks defined in Section 3.1. It contains 1,527 manually screened instances: 943 in VisSlideBench-Gen, covering text-to-slide, template-conditioned, and multi-image grounded generation, and 584 in VisSlideBench-Edit. Generation prompts range from short requests to detailed descriptions and structured style_json specifications, covering instructions from users and agents. Among the benchmarks compared in Appendix B.1, VisSlideBench is the only one that jointly covers all four creation interfaces, three prompt granularities, and task-specific measures of content fidelity, instruction compliance, aesthetics, and visual grounding.

sections.title: 4.2 BENCHMARK CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: Generation. VisSlideBench-Gen combines 493 cases derived from real presentations with 450 cases whose target slides are generated by Nano-Banana-2 (Google, 2026). The real cases preserve authored content and design patterns, while the synthetic cases broaden visual-design coverage. Following Section 3, we construct the instructions and visual inputs required for each case: no image for text-to-slide, one reference slide for template-conditioned generation, and one to four

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: assets for multi-image grounded generation. We manually screen target slides and instructions, removing slides of poor visual quality and prompts that are ambiguous or inconsistent. Editing. VisSlideBench-Edit uses subset of the editing data reserved for evaluation (Section 3.2); because these cases come from the same pipeline as the editing training data, the split measures indistribution editing quality (Appendix E). Each instance contains source slide, an edit instruction, and the corresponding target. We remove ambiguous instructions, invalid pairs, imperceptible edits, and severe visual artifacts through manual screening. The nine operations cover text modification, block addition and removal, background updates, changes to color, font, and typography, image replacement, and theme switching. Appendix B.2 reports task counts, source composition, domains, and editing operations, and describes how all cases are held out from training.

sections.title: 4.3 EVALUATION PROTOCOL
sections.content: We use OCR to evaluate text rendering and GPT-4.1 (OpenAI, 2025) to judge visual content, compliance with design instructions, and presentation quality. The criteria are evaluated separately before task-level aggregation; the text-scoring formula and additional evaluation details appear in Appendix B.3. Content Faithfulness (CF). We score text rendering with the normalized edit distance of Gong et al. (2025), adapted to the text the instruction requires (Appendix B.3). For multi-image grounded generation, CF additionally checks whether every required input image is faithfully preserved and appropriately incorporated into the generated slide. Instruction Following (IF) and Aesthetic Quality (AQ). IF measures whether the output realizes the explicit design requirements in the instruction, judged along Background Compliance, Color Palette Adherence, Typography Compliance, Layout and Position Accuracy, Mood and Atmosphere Match, and Block-Level Style Fidelity. AQ measures the intrinsic visual quality of the slide and is judged from the output image alone, without the instruction, along Clarity, Layout, Style Coherence, and Presentation Professionalism. The separation matters because slide can satisfy every design constraint yet remain visually weak, or look attractive while violating the instruction. Appendix B.3 defines each dimension. Editing. Adapting the SC/PQ framework of VIEScore (Ku et al., 2024) to slide editing, the evaluator receives the source slide, editing instruction, and model output to score Instruction Following (SIF), whether the requested change is applied, and Edit Consistency (SEC), preservation of unrelated text, images, layout, and styles. We define Semantic Consistency as SSC = min(SIF, SEC), so high score requires both. Presentation Quality (SPQ) uses the same four dimensions as generation AQ and is likewise judged from the output image alone. The overall editing score is SEdit = (cid:112)SSCSPQ.

sections.title: 4.4 HUMAN VALIDATION
sections.content: We assess agreement with human judgments using the annotation protocol of EditScore (Luo et al., 2026): two groups of two domain experts each produce consensus ranking of five anonymized model outputs per example, separately for each evaluation dimension, across all four tasks, yielding 2,153 valid pairwise comparisons. GPT-4.1 reaches mean Kendalls τb of 0.640, mean Spearmans ρ of 0.700, and pairwise agreement of 88.71%. Appendix B.4 gives the protocol and per-task results.

sections.title: 6.3 EXTERNAL BENCHMARK EVALUATION
sections.content: We further evaluate out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on two external benchmarks. On BizGenEval (Li et al., 2026)  (Table 2)  , which evaluates single-slide generation in the Slides domain, InfoVis reaches 46.0/79.8 on the hard/easy splits, the best result among all open-source models in this comparison and ahead of several proprietary systems. The remaining gap on the hard split reflects its knowledgeand reasoning-intensive cases, which slide-specific training does not target. On the Slides Aesthetics evaluation of SlidesGen-Bench (Yang et al., 2026)  (Table 3)  , the complete document-to-slide workflow described in Section 5 achieves an Aesthetics score of 27.09, closely approaching the best reported result of 27.28. This shows that InfoVis transfers from single-slide generation to end-to-end presentation creation with visual quality on par with the best reported systems. We report the Aesthetics track only; the content and editability tracks were not run.

sections.title: 6.4 ABLATION ON TRAINING STAGES
sections.content: Table 4 shows that slide adaptation does not transfer uniformly across capabilities. Stage 1 T2I-only CPT raises T2I Content Faithfulness from 6.29 to 8.00 but collapses editing Semantic Consistency from 5.98 to 1.60; four-task mixed CPT restores all four groups and lifts the overall score to 7.38. Shared SFT on text-to-slide data alone raises every group, including editing SC to 8.44. Each taskspecific SFT then lowers the overall score below the shared checkpoint (7.73). Part of the loss is cross-task interference: template SFT drops editing SC to 6.49. Part of it is shift within the task: the generation SFT pools are synthetic, and multi-image SFT lowers its own task from 8.50 to 8.12 CF, mostly on cases built from real decks (Appendix C.4). Weighted averaging keeps nearly the peak of each specialization (editing SC 9.13 against 9.19) while lifting the other columns, giving the strongest unified model (7.94).

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present unified framework for slide image generation and editing. We formulate four complementary tasks, construct large-scale slide-native training resource and introduce VisSlideBench for multidimensional evaluation. Trained on these resources, our model InfoVis achieves the strongest overall open-source performance on VisSlideBench, within 0.05 of Nano-Banana-2 and 0.42 of GPT-Image-2, and supports an image-centric document-to-slide workflow whose aesthetic quality is on par with the best reported systems.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used AI assistants in three ways. First, for writing and analysis: to draft and revise passages of the text under the authors direction, to check grammar and spelling, and to run scripts that aggregate stored evaluation outputs into the tables and statistics reported in the appendix; all research ideas, claims, numbers, and final content were reviewed and confirmed by the authors. Second, for literature search: to help locate related work and background material; every cited reference was verified by the authors. Third, as part of the method: language and multimodal models annotate and filter training data, synthesize SFT targets and benchmark cases, and serve as the automatic evaluator, as described in Sections 3 and 4. The synthetic data do not represent real individuals or observations, and the evaluators agreement with human judgments is reported in Section 4.4.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: Section 5 and Appendix C.1 give the training recipe and hyperparameters; Appendix describes the data sources, annotation and filtering procedures, and record counts; and Appendix details the benchmark composition, evaluation metrics, and human validation protocol. We will release the InfoVis weights, the training and evaluation code, the training data and data engine, and VisSlideBench.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Data sources and release. The real-slide corpus consists of talk decks that their authors released publicly and presentations collected from presentation-sharing and PPT aggregation websites (Appendix A.1); the synthetic targets are rendered by Nano-Banana-2 and annotated with Qwen3.5-27B and GPT-4.1. We will release the model weights, code, data engine, training data, and VisSlideBench for research use, with the source of every real-slide record recorded so that individual items can be traced and removed on request; the synthetic data do not depict real individuals. Human validation. The human rankings in Section 4.4 were produced by four domain experts in slide design and visual generation who ranked anonymized model outputs; the study collected no personal data from the annotators. Intended use. InfoVis generates and edits slide images from user instructions and supplied assets. Like other image generators it can render text that is inaccurate or misleading, and the document-to-slide workflow should be used with the source document at hand; we do not target generation of content about real persons.

sections.title: A SLIDE DATA ENGINE DETAILS
sections.content: A.1 DATA SOURCES, FILTERING, AND PARSING Generation sources. We collect presentations from two complementary sources. Academic data comprise talk decks released by their authors from CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, ICLR, ICML, and NeurIPS across multiple years. These decks contain substantial text, mathematical notation, equations, and data figures. The other source comprises decks from presentation-sharing and PPT aggregation websites across 39 topical categories, including business, marketing, education, technology, health, and design. These presentations contribute additional templates, color schemes, and graphic styles. The collected corpus contains over 72K decks and 2.2M slide pages. Deck filtering. Crawled material includes scanned documents, web or application screenshots, and nearly empty pages. We sample several pages from each deck and use Qwen3.5-27B (Qwen Team, 2026a) to assess slide authenticity and visual quality. The rubric accommodates plain backgrounds and dense mathematical notation in academic slides. We retain decks whose average score exceeds predefined threshold. Page parsing. We render each retained deck into page images at high resolution and parse every page with PaddleOCR-VL (Cui et al., 2025). Its Markdown/JSON transcription preserves reading order and recognizes text, mathematical formulas in LaTeX, and tables. The parser also localizes figures, charts, and tables. We crop these regions from the rendered page and store them as visual assets for annotation and conditioning. A.2 GENERATION RECORD CONSTRUCTION Text-to-slide generation. Each record contains an instruction and target slide image. We condition Qwen3.5-27B (Qwen Team, 2026a) on the slide image, OCR transcription, and localized visual assets. It produces short caption, detailed 300800 word description, and structured style_json specification describing page composition, content blocks, positions, and visual styles. The annotations describe visual assets in detail and preserve the recognized text. The generator receives the instruction without the visual assets. Template-conditioned generation. We pair each target with an adjacent slide from the same deck. Adjacent pages often share visual style while differing in content and layout. We sample template request from predefined pool and prepend it to the corresponding T2I caption, instructing the generator to follow the reference style. VLM checks consistency in background, color scheme, typography, and decorative style. It allows differences in content and layout; pairs below predefined threshold are discarded. Multi-image grounded generation. Each record contains an instruction, localized visual assets, and the original slide as the target. The annotation model receives the target image, OCR transcription, and assets, and produces the same three instruction forms. Its prompt requires the supplied assets to appear in the output and describes their intended placement. We retain pages with one to four assets and remove inputs whose shorter side is below 64 pixels or whose aspect ratio exceeds 8:1.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: A.3 EDITING PAIR CONSTRUCTION Each editing record contains source slide Isrc, an edit instruction xedit, and target slide Itgt. Seven operations are constructed by editing PPTX files; theme switching and image replacement use an image editing model. The latter two operations are reserved for SFT. Source PPTX files. We use both synthetic and real presentations. For synthetic sources, we extract text blocks from the OCR annotations of the T2I data and combine them with backgrounds from presentation templates. An LLM generates Python-PPTX programs that arrange this content into editable pages. We execute the programs and render the pages as source images. For real sources, we split crawled PPTX files into individual pages and retain both the editable files and rendered images. We screen sources for text overlap, element overflow, truncation, layout quality, and aesthetics. Only successfully rendered pages that pass these checks enter edit construction. Executable operations. For background updates, color changes, font changes, typography changes, and block removal, we generate rule-based atomic actions over PPTX elements. For text modification, an LLM produces structured action specifying the target element and its new text. PPTX editing engine executes these actions, and we render the result to obtain the target image. An LLM observes the source image, target image, and executed action to describe the actual modification. We construct block addition by reversing filtered pairs for block removal and generating new instruction for the reversed transition. Model-generated edits. For theme switching and image replacement, we first generate an edit instruction from filtered screenshot of real slide. Nano-Banana-2 (Google, 2026) then produces the target image, which we align to the source resolution. The replacement in the generated image can differ from the initial request. For image replacement, we therefore recaption the final source target pair so that its instruction describes the visual change actually produced. Pair filtering. We check for missing or identical images, unsuccessful operations, and invalid instructions. VLM assesses whether the edit follows the instruction, consistency between source and target, and the visual quality of the edited slide. Checks for individual operations include verifying that the new text in record for text modification appears explicitly in the instruction. A.4 SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING RECORDS Target synthesis. We construct shared pool of English 16:9 target slides from three content sources: concepts generated by an LLM across diverse domains, structured content derived from real SlideShare decks, and research papers converted into slide specifications. Nano-Banana-2 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image Preview) (Google, 2026) renders these targets using styles defined in prompts or sampled from curated presentation-template library. The resulting pool contains about 300K target slides. Generation annotations. Qwen3.5-27B (Qwen Team, 2026a) produces short instruction, detailed description preserving the rendered text, and style_json specification of at most 4,096 tokens for each target. These views produce about 890K T2I records. The template branch contains about 300K records across two forms of style supervision: styles specified in text and styles provided through visual template. In the former, Nano-Banana-2 first renders reference slide from the style text; in the latter, the library template is the reference. Both forms pair the target with this reference image. For multi-image grounding, PaddleOCR-VL extracts up to four charts, tables, or visual regions that do not overlap. Qwen3.5-27B generates instructions referring to these inputs. After filtering invalid crops and inconsistent instructions, this branch contains about 580K records. Editing selection. For the seven executable operations, Qwen3.5-27B scores candidate pairs from the editing pretraining pools for semantic consistency and presentation quality. We retain about 10K examples per operation. Theme switching and image replacement are excluded from CPT and used entirely for SFT, contributing about 40K and 30K records, respectively. Pairs for image replacement are additionally recaptioned with GPT-4.1 (OpenAI, 2025) to describe the edit realized in the target. The editing SFT pool contains about 140K records  (Table 5)  .

sections.content: C.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP DETAILS Training configuration. Stage 1 continual pretraining uses text-to-slide pairs for 13,500 steps with global batch size of 384. Stage 2 uses mixture of all four tasks for 16,500 steps with global batch size of 640 and at most four conditioning images per example. The T2I and templateconditioned SFT runs use global batch size of 640; the multi-image and editing runs use 768. Text inputs are capped at 4,096 tokens throughout. We optimize the diffusion transformer with AdamW (β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, ϵ = 108, weight decay 0.01, gradient-norm clipping at 1.0) at learning rate of 5105 for both continual pretraining and SFT, keeping the Qwen3 text encoder and VAE frozen. Stage 1 warms up over 500 steps from 107; later runs use 20-step warmup. Training uses BF16 mixed precision, gradient checkpointing, FSDP with hybrid sharding, one sample per GPU with eight gradient-accumulation steps, and seed 2233. Inputs are resized with aspect ratio preserved to an area of at most 10242 pixels and longest side of at most 2,048 pixels, rounded down to multiples of 16, so no single aspect ratio is imposed. The final model is linear interpolation of the four task checkpoints. Training resources. All runs use nodes of eight NVIDIA H100 80GB GPUs  (Table 11)  . sections.content: VisSlideBench-Edit is held out from the same construction pipeline as the editing training data, so it measures in-distribution editing quality; out-of-distribution evidence comes from BizGenEval for generation and from SlidesGen-Bench for the workflow. Aesthetic Quality remains the dimension with the largest gap to proprietary models, and knowledgeand reasoning-intensive slides, as in the BizGenEval hard split, lie outside what slide-specific supervision targets. Our generation SFT targets and the synthetic half of VisSlideBench-Gen are produced with proprietary model, which ties both the training distribution and those evaluation cases to its style; Table 16 therefore reports generation results separately for real and synthetic cases. Finally, the data and benchmark cover English-language slides only. Appendix illustrates failures in visual asset fidelity and the preservation of content outside an editing target.
